title: A Lie-Jordan Geometric Formulation of Lindblad Dynamics
authors: Leonel Bixano, Victor Alberto Cruz-Barriguete, Guillermo López-Alvarez, V. G. Ibarra-Sierra, José Luis Cardoso, Alejandro Kunold
abstract: We develop a Lie-Jordan geometric formulation of finite-dimensional open quantum dynamics, building on the algebraic framework introduced in our previous work (arXiv:2606.26477). The Hilbert-Schmidt operator space is endowed with an orthonormal Hermitian basis, in which the commutator and anticommutator are encoded by the structure tensors \(C_{μν}{}^λ\) and \(B_{μν}{}^λ\). Within this formulation, the von Neumann and Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan equations admit a direct component representation. Our central result is the identification of a basis-independent universal trilinear dissipative map, \( \mathcal D(X,Y)Z=XZY-\frac12\{YX,Z\}, \) whose components define a universal operator-space tensor depending only on the Lie-Jordan structure tensors. The physical dissipator is obtained by contracting this tensor with the expansion coefficients of the Lindblad operators and the Kossakowski matrix, thereby separating the universal algebraic structure from the model-dependent physical information. We further show that the combinations \((B+C)\) and \((B-C)\) generate internal left and right transports, allowing the elementary dissipative map to be expressed as a left-right bimodule action corrected by an ordered Jordan contribution. The universal map satisfies basis-independent trace and Hermitian-conjugation identities, from which trace preservation, Hermiticity preservation of the complete dissipator, and the reality of its component representation in a Hermitian Hilbert-Schmidt basis follow. We also derive its Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint and illustrate the formalism for a qubit with pure dephasing and amplitude-damping channels. This construction provides a tensorial and affine-geometric interpretation of the universal superoperator structure derived in arXiv:2606.26477 while keeping the algebraic and model-dependent sectors explicitly separated.
summary: This paper establishes a Lie-Jordan geometric framework to analyze the complex dynamics of open quantum systems described by the Lindblad equation. It achieves this by identifying a universal trilinear map that governs dissipation, thereby mathematically separating the general algebraic structure from the specific physical parameters (like coupling strengths). This offers a powerful, geometrically rigorous tool for analyzing decoherence processes.
main_problem: To develop a rigorous, basis-independent geometric formulation for open quantum dynamics governed by the Lindblad master equation.
main_result: The dissipative part of the GKLS equation is shown to be generated by a universal trilinear map, cleanly separating the model-dependent physical parameters from the underlying algebraic structure defined by Lie-Jordan tensors.
method: The authors employ an algebraic approach, representing operators in a Hilbert-Schmidt basis and utilizing the inherent Lie and Jordan structures (commutator and anticommutator) to decompose the dynamics into universal tensor components.
model_or_system: The system is general open quantum systems described by density matrices ($ho$) evolving under the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) equation. The formalism is tested on qubits undergoing pure dephasing and amplitude damping.

main_assumptions: The dynamics are assumed to be Markovian, trace-preserving, and governed by the GKLS equation structure.

paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the Lie-Jordan algebraic framework on the operator space to deriving a universal trilinear dissipative map. It then proves key properties like trace preservation and Hermiticity restoration before applying the formalism to concrete qubit examples, confirming the separation of universal algebra from physical input.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep structural understanding of open quantum evolution by mapping it onto established algebraic geometry (Lie-Jordan theory), which is highly valuable for developing systematic theories beyond standard phenomenological master equation approaches.
